sheet.name: Wren Ashgrove
sheet.opening: Wren Ashgrove, a half-elf bard of about nineteen with a quick grin and a sharper tongue, arrives at dusk in the river-market town of Marrowford, a few weeks after fleeing the caravan of her mentor Corvin Tallowmere. She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

At first light a second boat brought a tall figure in grey, who walked the causeway's far half, then returned. He was seen turning a ring on his left hand. Total on the far bank: six, plus the cloaked man. Wren's reed tell on the mooring stake was disturbed (reeds scattered). Marl was not detected. The Grey Cloak's plan likely: block the culvert from the far end and a boat behind the wagon at the turn of the tide.

entries.text: notebook: updated Gannet Causeway

You lean from Ember toward the wagon and murmur your warning. Corvin inclines his head. "Not a word, my dear. I'm all ears." Pell, riding on the other side, says to the sky that the gag is ready. Then you give the order and the column moves out at a walk, with Kit at your elbow and the six guards behind. You hum the road song low, and after a mile the guards are humming it too.

The ride is long and quiet. Your Perception on the way is a 9, and you notice nothing but gulls and wind. The tide-flats open silver ahead of you a little after half past twelve, and the causeway lies half-uncovered, a dark line over the shining mud, with the far bank hazy beyond.

The six guards peel off into the landward reeds as planned. Then Marl rises out of the ditch, mud to her knees, and gives her count in a flat whisper. Her stealth was perfect, and she saw all of it.

"A skiff landed at the boat-shed about two in the night. Sparrow, the brown coat, and four men. They went inside and stayed. At first light a second boat set down a tall man in grey. He walked the far half of the causeway and back, slowly, turning a ring on his left hand." She wipes her mouth. "Six on that bank, counting the grey one. Your reeds at the stake were scattered. They've used it."

So the master is waiting on the far side, as Corvin said. Most likely they'll block the culvert at the middle from the far end and bring a boat in behind you on the turn. The causeway opens fully around two, and it is half past twelve. You've three slots, three Inspirations, Kit, six guards in the reeds, Pell, Marl, and Corvin in the wagon with the lure in your saddlebag. What does Wren do?

At dawn on Day 18 a brown-coated man was turned from the chapel door at Thornhallow by Edric's men, who had been warned, and rode off along the river path.

entries.text: notebook: updated Sparrow

You thank the drover with a coin and draw Kit and Pell into the corner by the hearth. Pell doesn't like splitting the column, but he sees the sense. He picks two of his best riders and the fastest horses in the stable, and he promises to bring the wagon and prisoners at a steady pace. You pay a sleepy stable-boy a silver to take your note to Lord Edric on the best horse in the yard, and he is gone into the dark before you've finished sealing it: "Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." Then you check Ember's feed, count your three slots, and sleep.

You ride at first light, hard, with Kit and the two guards behind you, and Ember takes the road as if she's glad of it. The river runs on your left, and the fields go by in a green blur. You stop twice to water the horses and once to tighten a girth, and you reach Thornhallow at noon on Day 18 with a day's fatigue in your thighs but nothing worse.

The gatehouse is open, and the green and white pennant hangs limp in the heat. Lord Edric himself is on the gate steps with a cloak thrown over his shirt and Brother Osric at his elbow. Your note reached them before dawn, and the chapel doors were barred by sunrise. Osric tells you, in his cracked, half-deaf voice, that a lean man in a brown coat came to the chapel porch at first light with an arm held stiffly, found it barred, and asked for the priest as a pilgrim. The porter said nothing, and the man smiled and went off along the river path. "He was bleeding through the sleeve," Osric says. "I did not like his smile."

Lord Edric takes both your hands. His face is grey with sleeplessness, and under it there is relief. "You warned us in time, Wren. Come in. Tell me the rest."

It's noon on Day 18. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations. Pell's wagon with Corvin, Ansel and the prisoners is about three hours behind you. Sparrow is loose somewhere on the river path. And Lord Edric is waiting for you to tell him what you know. What does Wren do?

She was raised by him as a storyteller's apprentice, and she left in the night at a river crossing with his ledger of forged tales sold to nobles (its pages now hidden in the binding of her road-psalter), a few of his best forgeries, and a head start. She carries a brass lantern-shaped reliquary of the Lantern-Bearer, a gentle road-god of travelers and tale-tellers whom Corvin worshipped only as cover; it holds a curl of yellowed parchment in an unknown hand that may be a true blessing or another forgery. She does not know if Corvin has sent anyone after her. Her ideal: stories should be free, and truth is whatever people can be made to believe. Her bond: find the nobles Corvin cheated and decide whether to expose him or quietly fix what he did. Her flaw: she can't resist a secret, and she lies even when the truth would serve her better. She has 15 gp, a rapier, a dagger, leather armor, a lute, a diplomat's pack with blank paper and sealing wax, and was raised with no memory of her birth family. The hook: as she reaches the market square, she spots a caravan wagon with Corvin's painted shrine-lantern sigil parked at the edge of town, but no sign of Corvin. A frightened young page in a minor noble's livery is pressing a sealed letter into the hands of the wagon's driver, and the seal looks like one Wren has seen in the ledger. Something is happening that links her stolen ledger to a noble house, and it needs a quick-witted liar to either sort it out or be caught in it. Open on Wren in the square, with the choice of how to approach the wagon and the page, and a locked iron-bound strongbox on the wagon's tailboard that she itches to poke at.

input.add_to_description: Day 17 night: Wren sent a warning note to Lord Edric by the swiftest rider ("Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel"). Day 18 she rode ahead with Kit and two guards, leaving Pell to bring the wagon and prisoners.

entries.text: notebook: updated Sparrow

You thank the drover with a coin and take Kit and Pell into the stable yard. Pell objects once, that he was told to keep the prisoners in sight, and then he sees the sense of it. "Two of my best, then. Hale's rat has a day's start, and the wagon would only slow you." He picks the two fastest riders, a lanky guard named Dunn and a broad young one called Fenwick.

The innkeeper sells you a sheet of paper for a copper, and a tallow end for another. You write by the stable lantern: "Sparrow comes to Osric. Bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." You seal it with your wax and press the tin's impression beside it, so Edric will know the hand. A boy of the inn rides out on the swiftest pony with it, and the dark swallows him. You check Ember's feed, count your slots, which are full, and fall into a bed that smells of woodsmoke.

At first light you ride out. Pell and the wagon will follow at a walk. You go hard, with Kit and the two guards, along the river road, past mills and alder carrs, and you change pace at every milestone so the horses last. Nothing stirs on the road but carters and rooks. You raise Thornhallow's grey walls a little before noon, with the green and white pennant hanging limp over the gatehouse.

Tobin Reed, the page, is at the gate, pale and out of breath. He has plainly been waiting. "Your note came at dawn, mistress. My lord had the chapel doors barred before breakfast, and Brother Osric's inside with two of our men and a bolt on the door. No one in a brown coat has come to the gate." He swallows. "Though the smith's wife says a stranger bought bread at the ford at first light, and he held one arm stiff."

It's about half past eleven on Day 18. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots, three Inspirations, and 71 gp, 2 sp and 3 cp. The column with the prisoners won't arrive until later this afternoon. Lord Edric is somewhere inside the manor, and Sparrow is somewhere near it. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Day 17 night: Wren sent a rider ahead to Lord Edric: "Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." Wren, Kit and two fast guards ride at first light Day 18; Pell follows with the wagon and prisoners.

entries.text: notebook: updated Sparrow

You climb down, press a coin into the drover's hand, and draw Kit and Pell into the lee of the stable. Pell hears you out with his jaw working. "A wagon and two chained men will crawl," he says. "Go. I'll keep the prisoners in the middle of the column, and the barn fire taught my lads to sleep in their boots." He picks two guards for the ride, a lanky rider named Dunstan and a quiet one called Wick, and sees their horses are the best in the yard.

You write the note by lamplight on a sheet from your pack, folding it small: "Sparrow comes to Osric, bar the chapel and keep him inside the manor. W." You seal it with wax and your thumb. The landlord's boy knows the Thornhallow road and takes a spare horse and half a silver, and he is gone into the dark. You pay for a bed, check your slots (three still) and feed Ember a double measure of oats.

You sleep in a narrow room over the taproom with Kit across the door. At twenty-five past five the yard is grey and cold, and Dunstan and Wick are already mounted and stamping. Ember is saddled, the lamp-staff is across your back, and Pell stands at the wagon with a mug of something hot. The rider with your note has had a six-hour start. Thornhallow lies a long day's hard riding ahead, and you can reach it by midday if you push.

You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots, three Inspirations and 70 gp, 7 sp and 4 cp. What does Wren do?

input.add_to_description: Per Ansel (Day 18, unverified): Hugh did not drown. He married Joan, a chapel servant, in secret; old Aldous sent him away and struck the child's baptism. Hugh died abroad when Ansel was a boy.

entries.text: notebook: updated Hugh Verrel

You find Pell in the yard among the tired guards and tell him quietly: Ansel goes up first with two guards, and Corvin waits in the gatehouse under watch until you send for him. Pell grunts and points two spears at the stair. Corvin is walked off to the gatehouse. He glances at you and, for once, keeps his face still.

You walk Ansel to the study door yourself, his chain clinking on the boards. "He's ready to tell it his own way, my lord," you say. "Ansel, say it plain, and let Osric hear every word." Then you stand inside the door with your back to the wall and your hand on the lamp-staff. Kit takes the place beside you.

Lord Edric stands behind his desk. Osric sits by the lamp with the register open before him. Neither speaks. Ansel stops in the middle of the floor and looks at Edric's chin for a long moment. It is his own.

"I am Ansel," he says. "Son of Hugh Verrel, your father's elder brother, and of Joan, a servant at your chapel. Hugh did not drown at nineteen. He married her in secret, and old Aldous sent him away and burned the paper. He died abroad when I was a boy. Aldous had my baptism scraped and told the house I had never been. I was raised on a stranger's charity and I learned my own name from a dying woman." His voice does not rise. "I do not claim Thornhallow, cousin. I came to ask for a name, and I did it badly. I asked it of the dead, and of a girl who would not give me a lamp, and in the end of men with crossbows. I want that said in front of a priest."

Osric has put his finger on the scraped line. "It was scraped, my lord," he says hoarsely. "Not lost." Edric sits down slowly, like a man whose knees have decided for him. He looks at Ansel's scar, at the ring and at the book. "My father spoke of Hugh every feast-day," he says. "He never once looked up when he did."

It's a quarter past six on Day 18, and the lamps are lit. Nobody in the room has spoken for a while. Lord Edric is waiting, and so are Osric and Ansel. What does Wren do?

You ask Lyle to hold the chest unopened. If Dame Crowe's clerk arrives at noon, he opens it in front of her and a notary, and you'll be back by dusk. You have crossed the river on the same ferry and stand on the far bank by an abandoned hand-cart with nothing in it but straw. The track beyond forks. One way runs downriver toward Thornhallow. The other bends up into the hills toward Lantern's Rest and Ashby Weir.

You ask Lyle to keep the chest sealed until the clerk opens it before her and the notary. Then you take two fast horses from the bridge-house stable, and you, Kit and a watchman named Peg ride out the east gate.

The ride home is quiet.

You ask Lyle to hold the chest unopened until you're back. If the clerk comes at noon, he opens it in front of her and a notary. Then you and Kit take two fast horses from the bridge-house stable, with a watchman riding behind.

The rut doesn't help you. Your Survival is a 5. The market-day carts have churned the east road into one long muddle, and you can't tell which furrow is the hand-cart's. The gate-keepers are another matter.

At the east gate your Persuasion is a natural 20, and the toll-keeper practically falls over himself. He remembers the cart at once. It came through at dawn, pushed by two heavy men, with Sedley the clerk walking beside it and a lean grey-coated man with a notched ear riding ahead. He turns the toll-book toward you with a thick thumb. The entry reads: "For F. Oake, to Reedmarket wharf at Lowbridge." Lowbridge is three hours east by cart.

Then his wife comes out of the gatehouse, wiping her hands, and drops her voice. The clerk had stopped to buy a heel of bread, white as paper, and he pressed a sealed note into her hand. "For the warden, if I don't come back by the twenty-fourth," he said, and then he hurried after the cart. She has kept it in her apron since. She gives it to you, because you are the one who asked her kindly. The wax is a plain clerk's blob with a thumbprint in it. You haven't opened it.

It's ten o'clock on Day 20. You have 17 of 17 hit points, three slots and three Inspirations. The cart has a five-hour start on foot, but a cart is slow, and your horses are fresh. Lowbridge is three hours ahead. Dame Crowe's clerk arrives at noon, and Pell's wagon is still behind. What does Wren do?
